title: Monetary Policy Report—October 2024
summary: The Bank of Canada reduced its policy rate by 50 basis points to 3¾%, with the Bank Rate at 4% and the deposit rate at 3¾%. CPI inflation has fallen to around 2%, near the middle of the Bank's control range of 1%–3%, and is expected to remain close to the 2% target over the projection horizon. The Canadian economy continues to be in excess supply, with the labor market having softened and growth expected to average 2¼% over 2025 and 2026.
key_points: Bank of Canada cut overnight rate target by 50 bps to 3¾%, with Bank Rate at 4% and deposit rate at 3¾%
CPI inflation is now around 2%, within the 1%–3% control range, reflecting lower energy prices and weaker underlying inflationary pressures
Canadian economy remains in excess supply; GDP per person continues to decline
Labor market softening with unemployment increases concentrated among newcomers and youth
Canada's economic growth expected to average 2¼% over 2025 and 2026, supported by interest rate decreases
Global economy projected to grow around 3%; US growth strong but slowing; euro area subdued but rising; China facing property-driven weakness
Global oil prices have decreased and remain volatile amid supply/demand concerns and Middle East conflict
why_it_matters: This quarterly monetary policy report provides the Bank of Canada's comprehensive assessment of economic conditions and inflation outlook. The 50 bps rate cut signals a shift toward easing policy as inflation approaches target. Market participants monitor these reports for updated growth projections, inflation forecasts, and risk assessments that inform Canadian dollar and bond market positioning.
macro_context: The Bank of Canada has shifted to an easing stance after bringing inflation to target. With core inflation forecast to decline gradually and both upside and downside risks to the inflation outlook, the Bank appears to be prioritizing supporting growth. The excess supply in the economy and softening labor market provide room for further rate cuts. Global headwinds from China's property crisis and weak oil demand add uncertainty to the outlook.
